We examine three types of metric spaces: 4-dimensional Euclidean space, Planar graph metrics with Euclidean graph operations, and subgraph-free metric spaces that can be represented by finite graphs with a limited number of edges emanating from each vertex. For each of these spaces, any graph can be embedded into them with only minimally increased treewidth. In addition, there are some interesting corollaries for treewidth-based trealities and model theory.

In a smooth discrete dynamical system defined within the nonnegative orthant of R^n, a saddle point exists where its Jacobian matrix has zero determinant and certain eigenvalues possess positive real parts. Under these circumstances, nearby trajectories exhibit two distinct behaviors: as time increases, some approach the saddle point, whereas others diverge away indefinitely. Notably, this phenomenon can occur even when initial conditions are confined to the closed, nonnegative orthant, provided that a specific set of starting points facilitates approaching the saddle point while others result in unbounded growth. Further research reveals additional characteristics when global asymptotic stability cannot be achieved despite boundedness of trajectories.

The variational eigensolver uses adaptive circuits to study the ground states of quantum systems. Although circuits are typically designed by flipping qubits, a new approach based on flipping the system's lowest excitation has been proposed. We found this method results in shorter adaptive circuits, which always start with a fixed CNOT structure, allowing for greater NISQ resilience. Additionally, this approach is compatible with simultaneous angle adjustments and partial circuit fixing. We tested this method and compared it to the standard one by flipping qubits for two quantum systems: FermiHuber and Heisenberg models. We observed similar results in terms of ground state energies for both methods. We also showed that the method produces shorter circuits, which can be adjusted more efficiently. We found that all our circuits were more resilient to NISQ noise than the standard ones.

A widely accepted principle in a deep generative model is to use deep latent space
embeddings as a representation of observed data. However, there are cases where these
spaces fail to yield effective encoding or decoding performance. In this work, we
investigate the effect of using Maximum A Posteriori (MAP) estimates of embedded
values for the decoder instead of standard pointwise means. By achieving this through
probabilistic encoding techniques using low-dimensional data, we derive theoretically
sound results. Notably, introducing the Softestimation-Maximisation (SoftEM) module
to the variational objective demonstrates that it can be efficiently optimized.
By utilizing the full posterior distribution provided by SoftEM, we derive higher
quality models. Comparative evaluations on image and time series data reveal significant
performance improvements when using SoftEM in models such as VAEs and SREs.

The Hubble tension between local measurements and Planck's cosmic scale could be resolved by a low-frequency gravitational wave background, and this could potentially be sourced by a specific mechanism where the wave is amply intensified and confined within a fixed cosmological framework through a one-field inflation model incorporating an auxiliary scalar field, resulting in a residual inflationary gravitational wave background that matches recent findings from NANOGrav and other recent studies involving Advanced LIGO-Virgo observations. This research explores various models featuring an auxiliary scalar field, amending previous work and offering fresh prospects for the field of accuracy cosmology centered around the inflationary gravitational wave background. The accuracy cosmology approach, primarily proposed by Nakayama and Yoshida, involves a one-field inflation model accompanied by an auxiliary scalar field, allowing the inflationary power spectrum to be adjusted to match the cosmic microwave background and large-scale structure data, while the quantum fluctuation of the auxiliary field produces a gravitational wave background amply intensified and confined within a fixed cosmological framework, potentially resolving the Hubble tension and serving as a signal of a specific mechanism of the inflationary gravitational wave background that could be detected in future experiments, thereby offering a unique experimental opportunity.

Our observations, made using the Atacama Compact Array (ALMA) on July 1, 2017, detected a bright gas plume around the tail of Comet C/2015 ER61, as a result of water ice sublimation, which was located 0.14 ± 0.01 astronomical units from the comet's nucleus. The data obtained from the outflow indicated line-of-sight widths of approximately 1000 kilometers at 100 kilometers per second, 2000 kilometers at 20 kilometers per second, and 4000 kilometers at 5 kilometers per second. The emission patterns of water vapor were modeled using a source distribution function that varied with distance, and an observed asymmetry suggested the presence of a jet emanating from the comet's surface. Furthermore, our analysis of a spectral scan revealed the presence of water vapor and confirmed a constant rate of activity and composition of the comet's outflow over time.

We propose an unsupervised approach to the basic task of speech synthesis that operates without requiring speaker training, dictionary creation, or speech-to-text translation. It relies on a two-part system consisting of a noise-driven autoregressive model speaker, which converts acoustic signals into speech-like waveforms, and a speaker-independent no-verb decoder that translates these waveforms into spoken words. The entire setup is executed within the same environment as the speaker, enabling the decoder to learn from it. The proposed system successfully generates intelligible speech from a range of formant waveforms in both laboratory settings and real-world data, surpassing current techniques in speed and quality while providing a fast and scalable solution to speech synthesis that doesn't require labeled text data or speaker adaptation.

This article focuses on a crucial aspect of our understanding of the universe: the composition and dynamics of our accelerating universe, characterized by the universe's dark components. To investigate this, a Tsallis entropy-based holographic dark vitality model is considered for three distinct infrared cutoffs within the context of quintessence, a framework that includes a canonical non-canonical kinetic term with a specific potential. By minimizing the total energy, we derive the effective dark vitality potential and analyze its stable and unstable equilibrium points. Consequently, we examine the stable equilibrium points' properties in detail to determine whether they can account for the dark vitality's observed behavior. Furthermore, we analyze both the model and the matter field's evolution.

Multi-objective optimization problems are inherent to real-world issues and typically arise in real-time decision-making processes. In such instances where multiple, often conflicting goals need to be optimized simultaneously, finding an ideal solution set known as the Pareto front is crucial. A novel approach, combining the Non-dominated Sorting Genetic Algorithm II (NSGAII) and branch-and-bound, has been proposed to tackle multi-objective mixed-integer non-linear optimization problems. This method, motivated by evolutionary algorithms, incorporates intelligent local search techniques to yield superior results compared to its previous versions focusing on the entire Pareto front. A novel criterion, based on a local measure involving a normalizing factor and variable enumeration, has been introduced to efficiently identify non-dominant solutions. Additionally, this algorithm was applied to realistic decision support problems pertinent to the electrical industry, encompassing issues like optimal power flow, unit commitment, and design of microgrid networks.

We establish a groupoid and Lie algebra and their integral connections in synthetic differentiability. It is shown that any groupoid with Lie groupoid equivalence to a linked groupoid is inherently connected and further, is an integral connection for its linked Lie Lie algebra.

The availability of high-quality data has become a crucial aspect of breakthroughs in medicine, driven by an increase in research and diagnostic data due to advancements in technology and precision medicine. However, concerns regarding privacy and security hinder the widespread adoption of such data, as institutions are reluctant to share sensitive information due to fears of breaches and loss of control. This paper explores how implementing 'cyberinfrastructure gateways' can enable a seamless yet secure sharing of research and electronic health record data, thus promoting collaborative studies and accelerating medical breakthroughs.

In the realm of sentiment analysis, particularly for aspects, the explicit sentiment an expresser conveys about an aspect in sentiment sentences is not the whole story. Although clear, explicit sentiment is relatively easy to identify, determining the underlying, implicit sentiment proves to be a complex challenge. As a solution, we propose a pre-training strategy called contrastive pre-training to strengthen the aspect sentiment representation learning process. To this end, we first design a pre-training task called implicit sentiment inference, utilizing a supervised approach to improve expresser-aspect understanding. Next, we introduce a pre-training method called implicit sentiment mask for rapidly acquiring high-quality aspect sentiment representations. Consequently, our pre-training strategy yields superior performance over concurrent works across diverse datasets across various languages.

We examine computational methods for estimating the indirect effect in situations where the exposure variable is continuous, the mediator is binary, and case-control sampling occurs. To handle these scenarios, we developed identification frameworks for the indirect effect and its components, as well as mediation analysis formulas tailored to case-control samples, counterfactual case-control samples, and rare diseases. Through simulation experiments and data examination using the HUNT study, we evaluated the efficiency of our approaches in the context of rare diseases and investigated potential identification failure issues associated with the product-of-ratios estimator.

Multi-reconfigurable intelligent surface assistance, a cutting-edge technology, has the potential to revolutionize wireless communication by optimizing signal transmission in networks. Research into secure multiuser transmission systems, which employ multiple transmitters and receivers, has gained significant attention. However, real-world applications are hindered by practical issues such as imbalances in transmitter and receiver antennas' multiple-input multiple-output (MIMO) systems. To address these challenges, we develop a high-performance multiuser transmission design capable of accounting for MIMO imperfections, thereby enhancing the security performance of the system. Our design, specifically tailored to counteract MIMO imperfections, achieves superior results, specifically a theoretical maximum reduction in the peak encryption errors of up to 100 times compared to conventional transmission schemes through the strategic deployment of RIS. Extensive simulations confirm the efficacy of the proposed transmission design, showcasing its potential to significantly enhance secure multiuser transmission in real-world MIMO-limited networks.

This study explores a unique strategy of using contrastive value learning to improve how entities are categorized and evaluated within a dataset. By leveraging a form of retrospective summarization, our approach demonstrates the ability to effectively resample and relabel observations, outperforming conventional methods in handling various types of perceptions. We validate the efficacy of our strategy by applying it to both a synthetic environment and the high-stakes domain of autonomous driving. Moreover, our approach showcases potential as a versatile tool for future research.

Studies of solar breeze structures in the space surrounding Earth have offered insights into how the sun's weather influences the space environment.  A new, closer look at these solar weather patterns is now possible using the Parker Solar Probe, a spacecraft that has so far brought us nearly twice as close to the sun as anyone has before.  An initial study using data from this probe looked at four instances of solar weather patterns and compared them to what had been learned from observations made near Earth.  It was found that the predicted width of these patterns, when viewed from a spacecraft, would appear narrower, while their leading edges would look sharper and their internal structure would be more complex.  Furthermore, measurements made using this probe have so far confirmed an increased rate of energy transfer within these patterns, likely caused by the movement of charged particles and waves, due to smaller scale fluctuations.  These results provide important clues about how solar weather forms and evolves and will help scientists refine their understanding of space weather models.

In a quantum context, we define and analyze principal bundles with infinite discrete groups acting on C*-algebras. These structures arise when discrete groups act on local systems over manifolds. Furthermore, noncommutative principal bundles can be converted into fiber bundles with discrete groups as fibers through a specific equivalence relation. Additionally, we establish conditions for noncommutative countable principal bundles and investigate their properties in depth.

The study of cardinal characteristics of the continuum mainly focuses on how infinite sets within $[0,1]^{2}$ relate to one another. Two prominent measures, $u$ and $n d$, represent the smallest size of a collection of ultrafilters with minimal intersections and the smallest size of a collection of almost disjoint sets of integers, respectively. It is known that $n d$ equals the continuum, but the relationship between $u$ and $n d$ remains uncertain. This paper explores the interactions between $u$ and $n d$ by examining the cardinal invariants $d$, $t$, $r$, and $s$. The authors discover that $u$ is equal to $d$, $t$, $r$, and $n d$, which is an interesting finding. Moreover, the study shows that $u$ is equal to $s$, leading to the conclusion that $u$ is less than or equal to the continuum minus one, which is a significant result.

The concept of q-deformation, derived from higher mathematics, has numerous applications in physics, including fast light, slow light, and other areas in quantum optics. Researchers have applied q-deformation in various systems, including deformed quantum oscillators and optomechanical systems. This study focuses on examining fast and slow light phenomena in a q-deformed optomechanical system operating under the strong scattering and linear coupling regimes. We investigate how both the strong coupling of the cavity and the nonlinearity of the oscillator, characterized by the parameter q, influence the transport of light. Furthermore, the research aims to determine the effects of fast and slow light on time delays, clarity, and enhanced optical properties of the system.

Within the framework of the Dual-Rotors Model, which is a supersymmetric variant of the quark-mixing model, we have discovered the existence of negative mass modes in hadron and meson spectra when specific conditions regarding the hadron masses are met. Although the emergence of these unstable states is a natural outcome within our model, their prediction appears to be at odds with experimental findings, particularly in the context of the nucleon spectrum and baryon modes, raising concerns that the physical parameters driving the model may be subject to significant constraints.

A new method combines the power of deep learning with traditional numerical schemes to solve complex partial differential equations. This approach allows for implicit time-step calculations, making it particularly suitable for long-time simulations. By leveraging the unstructured nature of neural networks, the technique can easily incorporate inhomogeneous boundary conditions and a variety of time integration methods. Extensive testing on a range of equations, from the heat equation to the Navier-Stokes equations, demonstrates the technique's efficiency and flexibility compared to established methods. It's important to note that by employing standard numerical schemes, we can leverage existing libraries and theoretical tools for convergence and error analysis.

The ALICE experiment at the LHC is focused on studying the quark-gluon plasma, and its analyses rely heavily on the capabilities of its various subsystems. To enhance its data processing and analysis efficiency, a plan has been developed to upgrade the experiment's center-of-mass energy and luminosity per unit time beyond LHC Run 3's levels. This paper will detail the current status of the various ALICE detector subsystems and the enhancements that are being considered to boost their performance.

In the context of the Unruh effect, where an accelerated observer perceives a thermal bath of particles, we've discovered a geometric phase arising from entanglement between past and future light cones. This phenomenon challenges the conventional understanding of the Unruh effect and suggests it can be interpreted as an intrinsic effect of spacetime's causal structure. We've shown that by making measurements of Bell correlations between past and future light cones, one can derive the global unobservable field configuration. Furthermore, our model, in which an accelerated observer is treated as a quantum system, enables us to derive the orbital entanglement between past and future light cones, giving rise to the geometric phase. We've found that the accumulated phase is proportional to the ratio of the Unruh temperature and the observer's trajectory length. We interpret this effect as a time-domain equivalent of the spatial Unruh effect and provide a novel way to detect the timelike version.

Real-world system interactions often result in the significant challenge of
lost information, particularly in user event logging. These logs provide a
valuable resource for understanding system behavior, yet their interpretation
remains a difficult task due to a lack of event discovery techniques. Existing
methods primarily rely on English-only datasets, neglecting non-Western
languages. This study introduces a new multilingual dataset featuring
real-world English and Western Asian events to facilitate event discovery in
a range of human activities, including office settings, transportation, and
medical contexts. An innovative clustering approach, combining mutual information
and cosine similarity, is proposed to improve performance on both monolingual
and multilingual settings. A web-based interface for non-experts to assess
event grouping quality in a multi-dimensional way is also developed.

We establish a one-to-one correspondence between unitary representations of the special unitary group and globally generated holomorphic vector bundle representations, as well as a key equivalence between the positivity of global sections and the positivity of characteristic forms. Furthermore, we introduce generalizations of push-forward formulas for the total Chern class and Segre classes.

Our analysis examines the correlation between timing properties and spectral parameters observed during Hard States in Cygnus X-1, revealing certain connections that persist across various timescales. Contrary to a previous model, known as the Stellar Breeze, we found evidence suggesting an alternative interpretation of these relationships. The 1/f noise present in count rates and the interplay between photon index and count rate are linked to cooling behaviors impacting neutron star cooling, the accretion boundary layer, and the bremsstrahlung component, whereas counting statistics and Poisson noise influence other parameters like the Hump Fraction and isotropic flux. The Hubble constant was determined utilizing time delays observed in pulse phase, yielding a value of 89.2+9.8-10.3 H-1, thereby contradicting the model's prediction. The model's proposed feedback loop involving accretion torus radiation and neutron star cooling has not been detected, and its absence in Hard States presents an unresolved challenge.

The forking path for analyzing the ether-like term in various warm backgrounds is analyzed. Firstly, we investigate how this term impacts the thermal motion of protons. Then, we analyze the thermal leading order behavior of the thermal two-point function for both gluons and photons. Furthermore, we explore the influence of the ether-like term on the thermal two-point function of gluons when considering the finite number of colors limit. Lastly, we examine the influence of the ether-like term on the thermal rate of particle scattering for both photons and gluons. Furthermore, we investigate the scattering rate of photons in the limit where the number of colors is infinite.

A network of interconnected processors, referred to as Analyzers, collectively process a sentence to identify its grammatical structure and vocabulary definitions of the words within it. 
Unlike traditional methods that rely on assigning probabilities to various sentence structures, this approach utilizes a game-theoretic model where each processor evaluates potential sentence structures without assigning weights, and aggregates their findings to a common result based on the number of processors supporting each outcome.
Observations from experiments indicate that even a small group of processors can accurately identify legitimate sentence structures and extract meaningful information from them in real-time processing environments.
As these Analyzers gain experience, their ability to accurately parse both the structure and content of sentences improves, and they efficiently adapt to new or irregular sentence patterns and vocabulary definitions based on individual processors' contributions.
Notably, this approach demonstrates robust performance in handling noisy sentence content, and its parallel and distributed implementation allows for efficient scaling of processing capabilities to accommodate increasing complexity.
Furthermore, this shared understanding of sentence structures and content facilitates seamless communication between multiple processors, resulting in consistent and reliable performance outcomes.

The study of dynamic ejecta events occurring shortly after neutron star mergers has led to significant progress in understanding the physical characteristics of these events. Research suggests that the dynamical event can trigger a magnetized accretion disk which may generate an astrophysical jet. We have conducted simulations of magnetized accretion disks following neutron star mergers, taking into account detailed microphysics, to gain insight into the potential existence of magnetically driven astrophysical jets. We have found evidence supporting the existence of jet-like ejections occurring within hours after the dynamical event, offering a possible explanation for the delayed occurrence of certain gamma-ray bursts and kilonovae. The results of our simulations suggest that the magnetized ejecta events could be triggered by either the dynamical event itself or a smaller and faster merger product, such as a hypermassive neutron star. Further observational studies could potentially confirm the existence of these magnetized ejecta events and provide valuable insights into the physical processes occurring shortly after neutron star mergers.

A sample of 207 massive early-type galaxies was chosen based on their brightness and location in the sky, using data from the Hyper Suprime-Cam camera. These galaxies were then analyzed to determine the proportion of their light coming from tidal features, such as tails and bridges, as well as differences in color between these features and the main body of the galaxies. We found that approximately 10-15% of their light comes from these tidal features, on average, and that approximately 10-15% of their mass is involved in ongoing mergers, based on Hubble Space Telescope data. A strong correlation was observed between the fraction of their light in tidal features and their mass. Early-type galaxies with masses less than 10 billion solar masses were found to have a 20% luminosity contribution from tidal features, while those with masses exceeding 10 billion solar solar masses contributed only 8% of their light to these features, a statistically significant difference. These findings suggest that more massive galaxies may have formed their tidal features earlier and that our observations are consistent with earlier studies in the past ten to eleven billion years. Additionally, our findings support early major merger activity in massive galaxies as a way to explain the observed relationships in early-type galaxies.

A recent discovery of a class of stars exhibiting bipolar ejections has sparked research into the underlying mechanisms driving these phenomena. Our earlier proposed model, proposed in (I), attributed bipolar ejections to gravitational repulsion in regions of high density, resulting from the collapse of overdensities within galaxies. In this paper, we present an azimuthally symmetric theoretical model demonstrating how our gravitationally repulsive hypothesis can explain the formation of bipolar jets in star-like objects. Our findings indicate that overrepulsion within a rotating cloud of gas leads to the repulsive ejection of material along its rotation axis in the form of a jet, rather than a galaxy. In this process, a central dense core is surrounded by a rotating disk of material moving away from its path in the direction of rotation. The jet's trajectory is primarily influenced by the interplay between gravitational repulsion and rotation, as well as a material's distance from the core. Material closer to the core experiences minimal effects from gravitational repulsion, resulting in jets with increased rotational velocity, whereas material further from the core experiences material being flung off in the direction of rotation.

Recent research has shown that radio emission in millisecond bursts known as Fast Radio Bursts can occur over a broader frequency range than initially thought. Observations suggest that shorter wavelengths experience radio self-absorption, implying the possibility of radio emission occurring outside the observed band. By applying a two-band model, we establish an upper limit on concurrent radio emission in synchrotron self-absorption sources at frequencies below those observed. We find radio limits even tighter for thermal sources. Moreover, by considering time delays between different frequency bands, we explore potential radio emission at longer wavelengths and find it potential to constrain the cross-section of interactions between sources and their environments. We demonstrate the model's applicability to the well-documented FRB 20220912A, and emphasize the importance of multi-frequency follow-up observations of repeating FRBs.

High-power laser development relies heavily on 1D and two-dimensional (2D) theoretical modeling tools to enhance performance, enable rapid design of new lasers, and determine the underlying causes of experimental issues. However, these tools' utilization is often hindered by difficulties in accessing them or comprehending their operation. We've developed an open-source, user-friendly web interface that streamlines the integration of theoretical modeling packages, incorporating advanced features such as performance visualization, parameter optimization, and 3D diagram generation. The optimization feature automatically refines critical parameters, while the analysis feature investigates how to mitigate key performance limitations, providing analytical insights. The reverse engineering feature aids in identifying the sources of problems within high-power laser systems. We've successfully applied our optimization and reverse engineering features to analyze a Ti:sapphire amplifier, both a real-world example and a modified version with increased energy, and used the reverse engineering tool to explain an experimental discrepancy regarding thermal lensing. We've also applied our optimization feature to a glass amplifier to establish an optimal parameter set for achieving maximum beam quality. We've further expanded our optimization feature to accommodate multi-stage systems and have reverse engineered a Ti:sapphire amplifier to investigate thermal lensing's impact on its overall performance. We've shared our web interface's source code to facilitate its accessibility and promote future advancements in high-power laser development.

Current language models primarily create text, but in real-world scenarios, 
writers often utilize visuals for creativity and problem-solving. Models like GPT-3 are 
now being deployed in professional environments, requiring them to incorporate elements 
beyond text, such as researchers used for designers and writers. We aim to bridge this 
gap by introducing a new type of task where visual controls enhance creativity and 
efficiency through illustrations, sketches, and other visual cues. Our proposed model,
CREATE, integrates visual controls into text generation, combining visual and text 
processing capabilities. Experiments confirm its effectiveness, demonstrating that
integrated visual controls improve created content and allow for model compression.

We introduce an innovative transaction protocol called Delegated RingCT, enhancing the original Rivest's anonymous transaction protocol. The Delegated RingCT protocol significantly accelerates ring signature verification, yielding nearly linear scalability in the number of selected fake transactions. The enhanced performance can be further refined by employing public hash functions, thus minimizing the number of signature-verification parameters to a minimal set of five. The Delegated RingCT protocol necessitates a degree of user trust, as our trust analysis highlights the ring owner remains the sole potential threat of leaking real user identity under this framework. To mitigate this risk, a trustless deployment of Delegated RingCT on the Bitcoin blockchain is proposed, with real-world testing conducted using an implementation tailored to this environment.

A beam scan is a comprehensive study conducted by the ALICE O2 experiment's Interaction Region and Timing & Trigger System, checking the timing and synchronization systems and analyzing the proton-proton beam from the LHC. This scan generates several key parameters, such as beam intensity, transverse brightness, longitudinal phase area, and time spread. A recent beam scan was particularly interesting due to an observed rise in beam intensity and a corresponding decrease in transverse brightness as the beam current increased. This behavior, which couldn't be fully explained by standard analytical models considering factors like betatron tune shift and energy loss, was successfully replicated in a computer simulation taking into account inhomogeneous magnetic fields in the beam's central area. A notable example of such a condition is the presence of a strong solenoidal magnetic field.

In numerous scientific and engineering contexts, physical systems are represented using various models, such as those based on first principles, black-box methods, or black-and-white approaches. However, each of these approaches has limitations in accurately capturing the complex behaviors of these systems, particularly in cases where the models are incomplete or not fully understood. This research proposes a collaborative data-informed modeling (DIm) framework to resolve these limitations by combining multiple collaborative models that integrate black-box and black-and-white techniques, leveraging their respective strengths to improve accuracy. These collaborative models are trained using optimization methods that involve a transfer step, transferring information between them to ensure consistency and accuracy. This research explores the decay of the $\Upsilon(10753)$ into $\Upsilon(nS)\pi^+\pi^-$ where $n$ can be 1, 2, or 3, and it's assumed that this process is initiated by a hadronic loop mechanism. To account for possible final state interactions, the hadron triangle equations are employed. The output of this study provides the partial decay widths and branching ratios of the $\Lambda_b^+\overline{\Lambda}_b^+ \to \Upsilon(nS)\pi^+\pi^-$ reaction, which aligns with the observed data from the BESIII experiment. Furthermore, the results also indicate that the phase shifts of the $\pi^+\pi^-$ final state are primarily influenced by its final state interactions.

Quantized Neural Networks with limited precision can be effective solutions to complex optimization problems, despite traditional methods failing in such scenarios due to severe quantization errors. A proposed technique, referred to as AskewSGD, leverages a rotating coordinate transformation to navigate the distorted optimization landscape created by quantization and utilizes first-order optimization methods to successfully fine-tune quantized networks. An experiment was conducted using 1-bit and 4-bit layers on the MNIST dataset to demonstrate the efficiency of AskewSGD in comparison to other optimization techniques.

Model control techniques for manipulating soft robotic devices accurately in complex situations have garnered significant attention recently. These techniques rely on sophisticated mathematical and simulation models, along with optimization methods, to achieve precise model control for soft robots. This review investigates existing model control methods for soft robots and explores potential solutions for achieving efficient model-based control precision.

Our analysis of the Jacobi group is based on the concept of point transformations within the generalized elliptic Kronecker-Weber field $L(\mathbb{Q})$, specifically the field formed by values from the logarithm function applied to roots of unity. Consequently, the Jacobi group redefined in this context corresponds to a subgroup within the elliptic arithmetic congruence group related to $L(\mathbb{Q})$. This revised understanding aligns with earlier findings from our previous research findings.

Recent advances in fact verification have shown promising results, yet the current state-of-the-art approaches still struggle to accurately handle tables, mainly due to a lack of comprehensive benchmarks and difficulties in implementing table-aware models. To bridge this gap, we propose using table decomposition to verify fact correctness by converting the task into verifying individual facts. To establish this decomposition, we developed the Decomp property, which categorizes table facts based on their extractable properties. Our proposed Decomp property offers more fine-grained divisions than existing approaches, covering approximately 60% of the table facts across multiple datasets. Experimental results confirm the effectiveness of our Div property compared to existing division approaches, highlighting the need for incorporating properties when verifying complex table facts.

Recent advancements in general-purpose generative models, particularly spatially-resolved versions like image-conditioned generative adversarial networks (iCGAN), have led to significant successes. However, these models often struggle with detailed, non-visual conditions, particularly those that can be described numerically. To overcome this limitation, we propose the introduction of Hidden Space Conditioning (HiCon), a new approach that enables the incorporation of condition information into latent space of various spatially-resolved generative models, including iCGAN and iCGAN with external solver (iCGAN ES). The effectiveness of HiCon is demonstrated through experimental results, providing visual and quantitative evidence.

MCMC adaptivity can be achieved without adjusting chain length, as guaranteed under existing theorems.  Although being able to control the number of samples produced by the chain is advantageous, it is typically impossible to control the number of samples in adaptively tuned samplers like bridge sampling. However, this control is achievable in the context of the Bayesian logistic regression model using layered sampling, by carefully selecting sampling intervals based on specific quantiles of the chain. By doing so, all the generated samples can be obtained in a single pass, and any desired number of samples can be controlled. By employing weighted composite Markov chain adaption theorems and analyzing the error of weighted samples, it is shown that the achieved inference is equivalent to using unweighted samples from the same chain. Additionally, the proposed method is tested and compared in simulation studies with other adaptive MCMC methods in terms of computational efficiency and accuracy.

In a distance labeling system, every node within a given graph, represented as G, is assigned an integer tag that facilitates efficient computation of the shortest distance between any two nodes. Notably, binary tags have been found to suffice for certain classes of graphs, specifically planar graphs and graphs that can be embedded into a more expansive structure, known as the grid graph of a higher dimension. However, existing systems have significant performance limitations in terms of tag length and computation time. A significant limitation of existing systems is their inability to withstand faulty nodes. Our study presents a novel distance labeling system specifically designed for planar graphs, featuring improved tag length and computation time while demonstrating resilience against the failure of node faults.

In this theoretical study, we explore the dynamics of driven dissipative boson systems using a Bose-Hubbard model as a foundation. Specifically, we focus on sites containing multiple bosons and compare different driving and dissipation patterns within the model. We propose a novel approach to calculate the Drude weight for these multi-boson sites, which helps us examine whether these systems develop a superfluid state under steady-state conditions. We utilize the Keldysh chronology platform to solve the driven-hamiltonian dynamics of the model, which we then compare with previously obtained results from the mean-field method.

Recent research into out-of-distribution detection (OOD) has shown that neural networks can leverage probabilistic outputs to identify novel data patterns. However, existing methods have limitations, such as requiring extensive training or lacking the ability to balance performance with computational efficiency. A new approach utilizing a normal distribution, normal processes, and variational dropout technique has been proposed to output predictive probability distributions for neural networks, without the need for additional training. The results demonstrate improved latency and out-of-distribution detection capabilities on popular datasets, while maintaining competitive performance with state-of-the-art models. The code for this approach can be found on GitHub at https://github.com/abdulmohidin/out_of_distribution_detection.

In a finite Bose-Hubbard chain connected to reservoirs and subject to external driving forces, we study a system with tunable parameters. Our analysis using the Floquet-Markov approach reveals how weak non-condensing states can become stable and promote heating within the system. Under specific strong-coupling conditions, these weakly non-condensing states can facilitate quasi-condensate formation. The influence of noise is also considered, and our research identifies it as analogous to that of a dissipative quantum system with two distinct condensing states.

We focus our investigation on the Monge-Ampere equation's constrained right-hand side within a smooth, strictly convex $\Omega\subset\mathbb R^n$. As an intermediate step, we've refined Alexandrov's maximum principle for such equations. To establish our improvement, we employed an iterative approach, leveraging the literature's known H\"older continuity results for the solutions. Notably, our outcome implies the continuity, including at the boundary, of the H\"older continuous solutions to these equations.

Recent developments in statistical time-domain modeling have led to the creation of advanced, non-repetitive and stochastic (AANDR) pulses for timing applications, outperforming conventional hard-clipped pulses in resolving timing ambiguities and improving the timing performance of optical clocks. However, ambiguity reduction and Bayesian filtering can only process data on a case-by-case basis, while an alternative non-Bayesian approach using machine learning has been proposed for processing data in a more efficient, non-Bayesian manner. Nonetheless, this machine learning approach is limited to specific features of the AANDR pulses, while we present a new machine learning model capable of handling a broader range of AANDR pulses with both AANDR pulse width and pulse arrival time as input variables. Moreover, we demonstrate that an ensemble of such models can outperform the non-Bayesian approach for any given set of measurements, while also evaluating the feasibility of scaling this solution to more complex AANDR pulses with multiple sub-pulses.

In Service Function Chain (SFC)-based Software Defined Networking (SDN), maintaining reliable and efficient operation is a significant challenge, particularly when faced with unexpected failures.  Prior studies have addressed the issue of ensuring real-time SFC reliability during unexpected failures but have overlooked the severity of SFC reliability. Additionally, previous solutions have not considered the severity of failure, whereas a proposed framework in this research takes into account the severity of each failure and aims to minimize Service Function Chain reliability loss while ensuring fault tolerance. Taking advantage of Fog Computing nodes, which can perform both energy-intensive and latency-sensitive tasks, a joint approach is explored to optimize network resource allocation and energy efficiency. As a result, Fog Computing nodes are activated to support real-time SFC reliability under failure scenarios and energy constraints. Building upon existing solutions, two novel algorithms are introduced: the Severe Failure Propagation Algorithm (S-FPA) and the Non-severe Failure Propagation Algorithm (N-FPA), which employ heuristics to restore real-time SFC reliability during unexpected failures. Two corresponding Fog Computing node activation strategies are then proposed to optimize network resource allocation and energy efficiency. Two sets of simulations demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed solutions, revealing substantial improvements in average SFC reliability and network energy efficiency.

This study investigates the impact of loss functions by using "gradient surgery" to dissect specific components of loss functions that guide the training of neural networks. By analyzing the behavior of neural networks, we uncover how different loss functions behave and discover two essential properties that make a loss function effective: parameter independence and parameter orthogonality. We further establish theoretical boundaries for these properties and show how they can be used as a framework to evaluate and compare various loss functions. Following this framework, we systematically examine several existing and newly designed loss functions for image classification tasks. Our analysis reveals that many existing loss functions have limitations and does not effectively address certain challenges associated with neural network training. Moreover, we propose Soft-max $f$-divergence mini-batch independence (SOFI), a class of image classification loss functions that effectively addresses these limitations. Our experiments provide empirical evidence that loss functions within the SOFI class outperform their competitors and demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed framework in evaluating neural network loss functions.

We develop a new class of holographic tensors called hyper-invariant MERA, which allows for a efficient classical simulation of quantum systems across various dimensions by leveraging Schur-Weyl duality and the properties of finite groups. One example of this innovation is the Holographic Ising MERA, which accurately models quantum systems in higher-dimensional spaces with correlations that follow a power-law pattern. By utilizing Schur-Weyl duality, the Holographic Ising MERA exhibits explicit error correction capabilities under certain boundary conditions, enabling reversible bulk information retrieval despite potential loss of subsystem data. Furthermore, we extend this concept by creating a family of holographic tensors that accurately model correlations across diverse dimensions in a efficient manner.

This study examines the distances between adjacent filaments within the Galactic core by analyzing the distribution of inter-filament distances, focusing on its connection to the underlying spatial arrangement of filaments. We evaluated the distances using two distinct populations of filaments towards the Galactic core, obtained through two different methods, and compared them to those obtained from the underlying spatial arrangement through both Monte-Carlo simulations and theoretical probability density functions. The distribution of inter-filament distances differs from Poisson and Lognormal, yet shows similarities to Poisson when considering only bright filaments, although this association remains uncertain. We found that inter-filament distances were consistently greater than their corresponding mean distances calculated from the underlying spatial arrangement, particularly in cases involving bright filaments, exceeding the average value by a factor of 1.5. We attribute this trend to the mass-dependent filaments selection process.

Recent advancements in secondary distribution networks by utility companies have led to substantial reductions in electricity prices. However, some projects have failed to achieve their intended voltage improvement goals due to the absence of coordinated planning across network nodes. To address this issue, low-voltage networks can implement optimal and coordinated voltage regulation strategies. Typically, network operators rely on rule-of-thumb methods to set transformer tap positions, but our proposed approach integrates physical models to optimize preservation voltage systems, considering integrated primary-secondary distribution networks. By applying consensus algorithms, this method allows neighboring nodes to exchange information, ensuring coordinated voltage regulation. The performance of this algorithm is validated through comparison with an existing algorithm.

Multiarmed bandit theory often relies on the concept that agents can learn better actions over time, or "nonrandom," but typically assumes that agents' decisions are not influenced by timing issues and that all agents' choices are equally accessible. In contrast, we introduce a real-world scenario where timing issues are dependent on the specific actions being taken, and we show that this real-world situation can arise naturally from a context where "nonrandom" agents with timing issues independent of their decisions exist. Moreover, we introduce and analyze two different timing issues - "timing issues specialized by delays" and "timing issues with conditional independence" - which better capture a range of important multiarmed bandit problems. In both cases, we present efficient algorithms and provide bounds on the potential losses these algorithms experience, specifically, we demonstrate that both "timing issues specialized by delays" and "timing issues with conditional independence" lead to losses proportional to "optimal timing issues specialist with Arm-Independent delays" plus a factor related to the structure of the problem, where the timing issues specialist with Arm-Independent delays has limited timing issues and each timing issue has a bounded number of arms it can access, and we demonstrate that "timing issues with conditional independence" leads to losses proportional to "optimal timing issues specialist with Arm-Independent delays" plus a factor related to the timing issues with conditional independence, while our results are the first to provide nonasymptotic regret bounds that depend on the timing issues and the structure of the problem

Open-domain dialogue agents have garnered significant interest due to their
potential for enhancing human interaction experiences. The challenge lies in
creating natural conversational responses given the diverse range of possible
inputs and the limited scope of available data sets which fail to capture real-
world usage effectively. We introduce the concept of Structured Abstractive
Text Generation, also known as LEATHER, to generate more human-like and varied
responses. This approach enables the creation of infinite responses utilizing a
structure derived from first-order logic formulas, thereby ensuring grammatical
correctness and avoiding repetitions. Experimental results using the proposed
model on multiple datasets demonstrate its ability to significantly surpass
baseline models in terms of human-like response generation and the diversity of
answers provided.

This talk will introduce lattice QCD applications for simulating quantum chromodynamics under simulation conditions for temperature and baryon density above zero, focusing on a general description of the method for constructing Monte Carlo samples in finite density scenarios. We'll discuss how to overcome the complex sign problem, utilizing Taylor expansion and the imaginary chemical potential techniques for achieving moment calculations up to the order of the baryon chemical potential. Then, we'll present latest findings from lattice simulations, tailored for higher-temperature and high-density environments, followed by comparisons with experimental data and results from hydrodynamic models, with an emphasis on the properties of quark-gluon plasma and phase coexistence at low temperatures.

To achieve accurate predictions of complex physical systems, such as offshore wind turbines subjected to waves, wind, and loading, advanced statistical models are utilized. These models, however, necessitate a massive number of simulations for prediction, rendering them impractical for real-time control systems. Gaussian process regression is employed to create surrogate models, enabling the approximation of these interactions. By breaking down the interactions into multiple phases, Gaussian process regression is used to predict total loading on the turbines, surpassing the performance of the traditional black-box approach, according to recent research involving the OC3Hywind-MR wind turbine. By using Gaussian process regression to approximate loading predictions, researchers were able to significantly reduce the computational resources required, utilizing 50% of the training data from the black-box approach and yielding comparable predictions of mean, variance, and extreme values of loading sequences.

Social media platforms facilitate real-time global connection, and their analysis can yield significant insights into societal events. This paper investigates the impact of a 7.5-magnitude earthquake in Izmir, Turkey, by studying Twitter discussions. By geolocating Twitter posts using Geotwitterify and analyzing their sentiment using Sentimently, we developed a model to track how sentiment varied over time in relation to earthquake-related activity. Our findings enhance the comprehension of public perception dynamics during a natural disaster.

A group $G$ exhibits a property termed $R_\infty$ when, for every isomorphic copy of $G$ within another group $H$, $G$'s elements are swapped in a significant number of instances by an automorphism of $H$ towards $G$. In the context of two-parameter families of solvable Baumslag-Solitar groups $G_{m,n}$, research has shown that while the groups with $m \geq 2$ and $n \geq 2$ possess the $R_\infty$ characteristic with respect to monomorphisms, their subgroups can be embedded such that the resulting quotient groups lack the $R_\infty$ characteristic. A general strategy for assessing the $R_\infty$ characteristic for nilpotent quotients of solvable Baumslag-Solitar groups is presented in this study.

A direct and intuitive approach to obtaining a sturdy and accurate representation of a dynamic variable from limited and noisy data is provided by using a neural ordinary differential equation. This can be achieved by combining data-driven and physics-informed methods in a unified optimization framework that leverages the flexibility of adjoint-sensitive gradient calculations. A novel optimization algorithm is introduced that solves the inverse problem of inferring the underlying dynamic equation from time-dependent data. This method, applied to a transport problem governed by the Burgers equation and a reaction-diffusion-Adams-Bashforth system, demonstrates its ability to capture the underlying dynamics without making assumptions about the system's linearity or smoothness.

To accurately model real-world driving behavior, researchers require high-quality data that precisely captures complex details of the transportation system and the behavior of individual drivers. This study utilizes video data from the U.S. Interstate highways to create a comprehensive naturalistic driving dataset, which is then used to examine various driving behaviors within specific traffic scenarios. By applying advanced computer vision techniques, our approach achieves precise, automated tracking of crucial transportation system details, including vehicle types and road signs. Additionally, our study records various driver-related factors, such as age and gender, to provide a more holistic understanding of driving behavior. The resulting dataset can be utilized to answer key questions about how traffic conditions influence driving behavior and to identify factors that may affect driver decision-making in various transportation scenarios.

We've developed a novel concept known as reflected entropy in two-dimensional conformal field theories, and investigated its applications to boundary/conformal field theories, specifically to understand the geometric properties of spacetime with boundaries. Our research demonstrates that reflected entropy adheres to the strong subadditivity principle and exhibits a min-cut formula related to holographic states. By extending this concept to the context of spacetime boundaries, we discovered that reflected entropy provides a min-cut expression equivalent to the minimal disc area divided by the surface's boundary. This insight is further validated through the use of the cross-ratio of primary fields, and we observe that reflected entropy maintains the strong subadditivity principle in theories with boundaries. Additionally, we provide concrete examples and perform explicit calculations for reflected entropy in the case of the minimal model M(5,2), and also obtain general expressions for both diagonal and non-dional theories.

Recent research on a reconfigurable intelligent surface (RIS) has shown potential in enhancing the performance of wireless communication systems. However, phase noise in hardware and overlapping cyclic prefix in orthogonal frequency division multiplexing (OFDM) systems hinder RIS performance. To address this, a novel approach is proposed, where a compact OFDM-RIS user system is developed to negate the negative effects of overlapping CP and phase noise by modeling RIS coefficients in the time domain. Furthermore, an extended learning machine (ELM) time-series model is designed to estimate RIS coefficients, achieving superior performance, particularly in low signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) conditions. Simulation results confirm the proposed approach outperforms a basis expansion model (BEM) and short-term memory model, with a significant reduction in mean squared error (MSE) for the RIS-ELM method compared to the BEM-RIS scheme, especially in very low SNR conditions of 0 and 5 dB respectively.

This review examines the extensive research on the thermodynamic laws governing biomolecular systems, with a particular focus on the underlying statistical analysis. A key outcome of these studies is the development of a fundamental understanding of thermodynamic principles, enabling the derivation of entropy entropy and entropy flux entropy relationships, which serve as indicators of work and heat, respectively. Notably, these thermodynamic laws are universally applicable, regardless of the complexity of thermal baths, system non-equilibrium states, and system sizes. A notable breakthrough in this field is the creation of non-invasive measurement techniques, leveraging Brownian motion to accurately calculate energy consumption by weakly-coupled thermal systems. This advancement paves the way for precise energy efficiency evaluations in thermal machines, cellular systems, equilibrium systems, and nonequilibrium systems.

We are examining the deformation theory of G2-instantons on nearly G2-manifolds. Given a nearly G2-manifold with metric g, we look at the complex vector space representing the tangent space of the space of G2-instantons. This space is defined as the kernel of the linearized equation for G2-instantons. We then analyze the nearly G2-deformations and find a decomposition of this space into three distinct subspaces: Calabi-Yau three-fold deformations, K3 deformation, and nearly G2-deformation. We specifically investigate the deformation space on a 7-sphere in the context of the Taub-NUT fibration over T6, where we decompose the space into three nearly G2-deformations and to find the baryon deformation, we investigate the space on the twisted torus, where we found that the space is identical to the baryon deformation on the fibration of T6.

The widespread use of COVID-19 symptoms and contact tracing has been made possible by an app, which aims to help the public health by monitoring infections in real time. To achieve this, users install an app that generates a unique cryptographic key, which is then shared with a secure central server on a daily basis. When a user gets infected, their signature is sent to a special verification server, which only accepts valid information from certified medical personnel. By signing each contact report with a cryptographic key, only authorized health agencies can access user information, which is then stored on a central verification server. To analyze system security, we modeled interactions between a user and the system as a Markov process, which allows us to study how likely it is for user privacy to be compromised based on app design and parameters. Our research shows that user privacy can be compromised if their interactions with the contact tracing system are changed, which in turn affects their infection status. By applying a technique called mean-field analysis, we were able to derive an analytical expression that predicts how likely user privacy breaches are, which was later validated by computer simulations.

Recently, various machine learning algorithms incorporating quantum components have been suggested in order to potentially achieve an quantum advantage for encoding classical data but without success in up to date experiments. In this work we propose a different method for the quantum encoding process by using the properties of an ideal quantum memory instead. We demonstrate that this new approach can in theory result in an quantum advantage by using examples that show increased success rates in complex quantum-machine learning classifications compared with an idealized yet unrealistic encoding technique. We also show that this quantum encoding method is more realistic than previous ones by accounting for some fundamental aspects of quantum mechanics, for example entanglement, coherence and decoherence, yet still maintaining the possibility of achieving a quantum advantage.

This work introduces a tool that generates executable C code and a accompanying proof of its correctness, expressed in ACL2. The tool was created through a framework that enables shallow embedding of C within ACL2, allowing direct representation of C properties. This specific tool was formulated to satisfy the requirements of the KeYring distributed key management library, and can be adapted to other projects.

A cluster of faint asteroids comprising the (39991) Iochroma group occupies specific J2 resonances with Jupiter, with three of their five J2 resonances located between 4.1 and 4.7 AU. Our research examines Iochroma group dynamics within these resonances through numerical modeling of long-term evolution in the key 3-jupiter-5-nu-la-longitude-keyresonanceandoutsideofit,aswellasinresonanceswithJupitermoonIcarus within Phoebe's orbit and beyond the Iochroma group's boundaries, in Icarus's resonance. We evaluate Iochrauomagroupbehaviorinresonancesandinfreeorbitevolutionsandcompareitstoastrophysicalsecularresonancemodels,whichsuggestedsecularresonancesasapossibleoriginfortheIochromagroup. Connection formulas for the Hurwitz Zeta functions $\zeta(s, \alpha)$ and $\zeta(s, 1-\alpha)$ at positive integer values $s$ are revisited. A suitable evaluation of these connection formulas enables us to establish a general theorem superseding Ramanujan's famous result on the odd zeta values.

We demonstrate that for a closed semi-simple Lie group V, the logical circle-equivariant elliptic cohomology of the projective space formed by the quotient of V by the center Z is equal to a direct sum of cohomology groups related to maximal torus classifying spaces. This new theory expands upon previous equivariant cohomology theories that have already been studied for topological groups.

We examine specific physical models where we apply a novel machine learning approach to extract and utilize information from a mathematical structure to make precise predictions about the models and uncover their hidden properties. By implementing a machine learning method based on CW complexes to map the relationships between their components and distributions, we successfully predict physical model data with high accuracy in two tested scenarios. The first scenario involves employing this machine learning method to simulate Ising models on various 2D graphs within the Manhattan circle of radius three, using an encoding of the complex's 2D grid structure to accurately model the spin configuration distributions, resulting in excellent predictions of both marginals and joint distributions. The second scenario involves using this machine learning method to simulate 3-valent quantum Ising models on the unit 3-sphere, leveraging an encoding of the sphere's CW complex structure to accurately predict both marginals and joint magnetization distributions. Moreover, this machine learning approach enables us to identify and analyze the correlations within spin configurations, revealing that the interactions between spins decay exponentially with increasing distance between sites.

To further comprehend the mechanisms governing $J/\psi$ production in next-to-leading-order (NLO) $e^{+}e^{-}$ interactions, a thorough analysis has been conducted to investigate the properties of $J/\psi$ polarization states in various reactions. By comparing the results of $e^{+}e^{-} \to J/\psi + \eta_c$ and $e^{+}e^{-} \to J/\psi + \chi_{cJ}$ reactions with the data from the BESIII experiment, the research found that $m_{b}$ and $m_{c}$ values, including their uncertainties, can be precisely determined using the NLO electromagnetic annihilation amplitudes for $^3S_1^{[8]} \to J^\psi$ and $^3S_1^{[1]} \to J^\psi$ transitions. Moreover, the study discovered that $e^{+}e^{-} \to J/\psi + \eta_c$ reactions are affected by both color-octet and color-singlet contributions in an inseparable manner, in contrast to $M[8]\ll M[1]$ assumptions and it has been verified that the amplitude for $e^{+}e^{-} \to J/\psi + \chi_{cJ}$ is dominated by the color-octet contribution. By employing the NLO calculations, $m_{b}$ and $m_{c}$ can be determined with high accuracy

This study examines how enthusiastic signal users employ their passwords, or PINs, on the signal messaging app. The research reveals that some users, including those who are highly engaged, are unsure of the rationale behind their PINs. The average number of PIN characters used by signal users is just 4.25, significantly below the optimal level of complexity. Notably, some users leverage encryption features like secret chat and hidden chats, yet use weak PINs that can be easily guessed.

As the cost of solar energy continues to decline, its share in the energy mix is expected to rise, necessitating more accurate methods of calculating the weighted integral of solar energy with respect to time. Existing solar-energy integration techniques often lack precision or rely on approximations that compromise their reliability. We propose a novel approach, known as solar-weighted Gaussian quadrature, which significantly enhances the precision of numerical solar-energy integration without incurring additional computational costs. Unlike the traditional Gaussian quadrature method, our approach takes into account four key parameters - weight, center, scale, and shape, yielding a quadrature formula that accurately reflects the varying energy supply patterns throughout the day. We validate the effectiveness of our method through both theoretical proofs and empirical case studies conducted over multiple years. Our results demonstrate that the proposed quadrature formula can enhance the approximation error by up to two orders of magnitude compared to the traditional Gaussian quadrature method. We also employ this method to investigate the impact of adding more nodes to the traditional quadrature formula.

Recent research has shown that curvilinear coordinate systems, such as those implemented in finite elements, can enhance the accuracy of optimization methods like Newton and quasi-Newton. However, these methods currently face challenges due to coordinate transformations used to express tensors in Cartesian coordinates. This challenge is successfully addressed by the ViViT framework, which utilizes the principles of differential geometry to maintain curvilinear coordinate benefits while overcoming these challenges. ViViT incorporates the generalized Gauss-Newton's diminished structure, enabling in-situ tensor computations and eliminating the need for coordinate transformations. Furthermore, ViViT facilitates the use of advanced data structures, such as the Compressed Sparse Row format, to scale the methods presented in this research. These breakthroughs enable the successful application of geometry-aware optimization methods within complex scientific simulations.

In languages where gender is prevalent, such as in 4-5 billion speakers, meaningful gender assignments prevail rather than merely grammatical ones.  This phenomenon is particularly notable in Spanish, a language that marks gender through determiners and articles.  Our study delves into the gender-assignment system of Spanish, assigning gender to all nouns occurring in the Billion Words Corpus of Spanish, and utilizes these assignments as targets to train a gender-bias-aware neural network.  By incorporating these assignments into our multilingual BERT model, we examine the gender influence on representation characteristics of nouns in Spanish as well as their influence on representations of unrelated nouns with unknown gender.  Our results demonstrate that Germanic and Romance gender biases significantly impact the representation of individual nouns, regardless of their gender assignment, and influence correlations between their representations and external semantic and sociodemographic factors.

From individual elements to complex groups, a Riemannian manifold's volume growth can be understood, and its underlying structure can be inferred. A key finding demonstrated by Cheeger and Gromov that the presence of a non-trivial fundamental group leads to the existence of a higher-dimensional de Rham cohomology class, invariant under volume growth, is a pivotal point. Additionally, the notion of finiteness dimension was introduced, which establishes an upper limit on volume-invariant cohomology classes. Building upon these concepts, a new finiteness dimension criterion was sought that could be experimentally applicable to the rational points of a charmable, irreducible symmetric space, specifically one where the points have integer homology characteristics. A group with these features, along with its uniform lattice group, would then satisfy the finiteness dimension criterion, with specific bounds on its homology classes in relation to its rank.

We introduce an innovative approach to object pose estimation that involves learning and predicting the pose of an object category without requiring explicit 3D pose annotations in the training data. This challenge is particularly relevant in robotics, where objects are often encountered without prior knowledge. This study focuses on the large-scale everyday scene for learning object poses and explores a new, annotation-efficient learning framework. This framework leverages knowledge transfer from a set of annotated categories to a new, unseen zero-shot category. This study formulates the task as a multi-step object reconstruction problem, where the pose of the new category is inferred by reconstructing 2D images of the object. This study presents two key components: (1) auto-3D pose exploration, where pose priors for 3D objects are obtained from the COCO dataset, and (2) 3D pose transfer for the object category of interest. This study also introduces a self-supervised learning framework for 2D object reconstruction, which can be used to refine the reconstruction process. This study demonstrates the effectiveness of the proposed framework on the ROBO-SETY dataset, which consists of over 1,000 sets of images with diverse 3D pose annotations. This study shows that the proposed framework significantly outperforms existing methods, with a significant improvement in ZPCK accuracy, especially on challenging scenarios. Traffic forecasting, a crucial task for smart city development, has been a significant research focus in the last decade. Recent advancements in traffic forecasting have primarily focused on enhancing accuracy through advanced network architectures, often neglecting the importance of extracting meaningful features from existing data. Previous methods have relied on a diversity of feature extraction techniques, but due to traffic data's inherent non-uniformity, these methods have been limited in effectiveness, often resulting in inaccuracy and inefficiency. To address these challenges, a new approach called SimFE has been developed. SimFE uses sparse traffic data and employs similarity-based analysis to extract features dynamically, which in turn improves the overall forecasting accuracy and efficiency. Through extensive testing with real-world sparse traffic datasets, SimFE has outperformed existing state-of-the-art methods in both precision and speed.

This research explores how variational graph autoencoders (VACAs) can be used to learn the causal structure of complex systems through causal counterfactuals. VACAs are shown to effectively recover causal structures in random graphs, even when there are unobserved variables influencing the system. Causal VACAs can also be used to answer questions about what variables would happen in hypothetical situations, by estimating causal relationships using limited information about graph structure. We tested VACAs on synthetic data sets to see how well they work compared to other methods, including structure learning from data without interventions. Our results indicate that VACAs can accurately learn causal structures and make accurate predictions about causal relationships.

Transient phenomena have been a key focus of radio astronomy research, with an increasing need for real-time processing and analysis. The Irish LOFAR station has recently incorporated real-time capabilities, including a dedicated single polarization antenna and a custom multi-beam system, to enhance detection rates. These components belong to the REAL-time Advanced Electromagnetic Antenna and Transmitter Array (REALTA) project, which also incorporates a advanced transmitter system. This article presents initial results from the Real-time Transient Capture (REALTC) algorithm, which utilizes the REALTA and aims to identify radio bursts at 336 MHz. With a 15-minute integration time, REALTC has successfully identified 294 events, including 229 single-pulse events and 65 clustered pulses. This represents a considerable number of events for real-time algorithms and at least ten times more than previously recorded in scientific data, indicating the value of real-time capabilities in radio astronomy.

Research in physics is increasingly accelerated by computational tools, 
particularly artificial intelligence and machine learning techniques. Although 
metaphotonics is a well-established field, its integration with such 
computational tools is relatively underexplored. Our review highlights key 
metaphotonics concepts that are amenable to AI/ML enhancements. 
Specifically, we propose potential AI/ML enhancements in the areas of 
nanoplasmonics, photonic crystals, and guided wave photonics, and 
identify areas of intersection between metaphotonics, plasmonics, and 
quantum optics. Furthermore, we discuss the necessity of developing new 
metamaterial properties inspired by the capabilities of computational tools.

The film industry generates a massive global revenue, yet a significant challenge remains in predicting movie success before and after release. Using a large, comprehensive dataset covering American films from 1925-2018 and including 2019 films at the prediction's time, this study explores the impact of pre-release attributes on revenue. A time-based split of the data into training and testing sets is used to create more realistic predictions. Initially, the study examines the income distribution of these movies, revealing a skewed towards lower earnings. Next, the research identifies key factors such as genre, star power, and running time that influence movie revenue. Notably, the findings suggest that movies receiving pre-release predictions often exceed their actual revenue in 90% of cases. To accurately represent this phenomenon, regression models are applied, with notable improvements seen in utilizing content-based features from film reviews.

This work examines the stabilization of a grid segment with and without auxiliary auxiliary frequency regulation in the presence of significant share of non-controllable renewable energy sources.  We focus on the auxiliary frequency regulation as opposed to primary frequency regulation as the former employs finer actuators for enhanced control.  This finer control can contribute positively to grid stability.  This control theory model utilizes two variables to describe the grid's operating point - node voltage and frequency.  This theoretical model is an extension of the traditional two-variable model designed for grids without significant share of non-dispatchable renewable energy.  The model is constructed by merging auxiliary frequency regulation with the conventional primary frequency regulation.  This framework is used to analyze the impact of the auxiliary frequency regulation on grid stability, with simulations grid stability.  This analysis is performed using energy-bus modeling and validated using detailed time-domain grid simulations grid stability.

The integration of computing, communication, and electronic systems into physical entities such as vehicles, machinery, and power grids creates interconnected cyber-physical systems (CPS). When multiple CPS are linked, they form a vast network referred to as a cyber-physical network of networks (NPNet). To manage these complex networks, intelligent agents embedded within individual components can adapt and optimize the overall system, creating a self-regulating framework. This paper examines the implementation of intelligent agents within NPNet to enhance overall performance, utilizing a network of power generators and consumers as a concrete example to illustrate this concept.

Blazars, a type of active galactic nucleus, are known for their extremely bright and variable spectra across various wavelengths.  Analyzing the light curves and spectra of 11 European Southern Observatory (ESOTIC) blazars revealed distinct patterns in their light curves, with significant changes in the optical and near-UV (NUV) bands, and no such changes observed in the X-ray band.  These changes were observed within 10-100 second time scales, and were constrained by 10% light curve fluctuations.  Moreover, 8 out of the 11 blazars in this study were found to have rising spectra with indices ranging from 0.2 to 2.1, characterized by a parameter alpha_E less than 1.5, indicating a lack of X-ray dominance.  This phenomenon, known as the "UV Excess" or "UV Excess Anomaly," poses a significant challenge in understanding the physical properties of blazars.  Utilizing a Monte-Carlo code called MAPPIES, we studied the NUV to X-ray continuum emission of blazars, and found that the majority of the emission in this energy range is produced by a single component located within the jet, undergoing external Compton scattering.  This component interacts with a radiation field primarily composed of synchrotron photons, and produced most of the emission observed in the NUV to X-ray range.  However, adding a second

We have developed an analytical method to extend the sampling trajectory across complex terrain. This approach utilizes a least-squares method to fit a smooth mathematical model to the complex terrain's elevation. By increasing the sampling rate near these areas and applying a similar technique to other features, such as cliffs, we can optimize data collection for various atmospheric measurements. Our method has been successfully applied to height maps and wind speed data and can be adapted to other characteristics. An open-source implementation of our algorithm is available on GitHub.

This research focuses on a type of pure quantum state known as symmetric states, which are composed of two orthogonal subspace components weighted by a parameter t. Traditional methods for identifying complex states like GHZ states utilize the minimum number of measurements and reveal correlations. In contrast, we propose a more comprehensive, systematic framework to extend the concept of minimal measurement sets, enabling precise state identification in complex systems. Our method is demonstrated through practical two-qubit examples and further validated through simulation of the identification process for a three-qubit case.
