SoftEngDerive is a Java-based program that converts unstructured text into Java code, facilitating the development of software documentation and program comments.

In a downlink network, multiple base stations and mobile devices are connected, and a need arises to recover original data at the destination. To achieve this, network coding is a technique that combines data packets and allows recipients to retrieve the original information using cooperative transmission through relay stations. Focusing on a scenario with binary downlink packets and an objective to minimize power consumption, the task involves determining packet collaboration and optimizing power distribution among the base stations and relays. A joint approach to analyzing relay allocation and network coding collaboration leads to an objective function with properties conducive to an efficient solution method, resulting in a polynomial-time algorithm along with performance guarantees expressed in terms of an approximation ratio. To further simplify the problem, a relay allocation policy that depends only on the link quality between base stations, relays, and mobile devices is proposed, and a collaboration scheme that ignores base station locations and focuses solely on binary packet demands is examined. For comparison, a benchmark case involving continuous demand vectors and the absence of base stations is also considered.

Recently, a novel principles-based DFT method was introduced, enabling the study of superconductivity in materials at the atomic scale. A key focus of this approach is the examination of localized disorder within superconductors, resulting in the emergence of localized states in energy gaps that typically house no states. In this work, we apply the principles-based DFT method to research Yu--Shiba--Rusinov (YSR) states formed when a magnetic Mn adatom and dimers are placed on top of a d-wave superconducting Nb(110) surface. The analysis reveals a significant reduction in YSR level splitting for Mn dimers, specifically by a factor of 20 compared to individual Mn adatoms. Furthermore, our findings suggest a universal characteristic in YSR states for both Mn adatoms and dimers, characterized by four distinct states and the presence of two nearly equal-energy pairs. These YSR states exhibit a notable dependence on the orientation of Mn moments, and it is discovered that they also affect the local spin polarization of surrounding Nb atoms.

A preliminary study was conducted utilizing the decay-in-flight technique to find $K^+\rightarrow\pi^+\nu\bar{\nu}$. Based on this experiment, we observed no evidence of the decay and set a 90% confidence level upper limit on its branching fraction at $4.2\times10^{-7}$. This result is the first one obtained from an experiment that uses the decay-in-flight technique, though it is less sensitive compared to the stopping experiment by NA48/K2K.

Scan matching algorithms face challenges in overcoming existing search ranges and avoiding biased results due to their scoring methods. Research has revealed that conventional methods are susceptible to search bias, which affects their performance. In particular Distribution-driven Deep Neural Network (DNN) models are prone to this issue. This study introduces a strategy to reduce search bias in DNN-based scan matching algorithms by using a filter based on the entropy of the score map to expand the search area's effectiveness. The proposed method has been tested on various scenarios, including noisy and large-range scenarios. Results show that it significantly improves accuracy in noisy conditions and outperforms other models in large-range scenarios.

We introduce an innovative approach for satellite image edge identification that overcomes the limitations of deep networks, including the need for significant memory and high energy consumption. Unlike deep networks, which often fail to generalize well beyond their training data, we demonstrate that a simple model can achieve comparable accuracy on diverse datasets, as evidenced by low training loss that translates to external datasets. Our accuracy is further validated by human evaluation and quantitative metrics like PSNR and SSIM. Additionally, we analyze the performance of our model across different resolution inputs and analyze the training process to reveal its simplicity and effectiveness.

High-fluence x-ray absorption edge spectroscopies utilize x-ray free electron lasers to study materials with an exceptionally large number of photons. This high photon count generates substantial ionization levels, resulting in complex internal many-body states that are challenging to interpret data from these experiments. The escalating ionization in materials causes spectral distortions that hinder the application of standard extended x-ray absorption fine structure analysis methods typically used for experiments with lower photon counts. These distortions are largely attributed to non-radiative ionization processes, such as the autoionizing effect and the meissner effect, which are exacerbated by the initial photon density and persist over a range of time periods, commencing with a period of femtoseconds and extending into microseconds or even milliseconds. To address these complexities, a framework of rate equations is proposed, which accounts for the interplay of various ionization and electron migration mechanisms that occur within the material. This new framework enables a novel type of x-ray absorption edge analysis, which incorporates features such as the meissner effect and provides insights into important parameters such as the initial ionization yield and the degree of non-linear ionization. This type of analysis has been successfully implemented in this study, which evaluates its effectiveness using simulated x-ray absorption edge spectra generated with an adaptation of the core-hole model.

This paper introduces the concept of GMPADCA, which is the first framework to evaluate the modulation categorization (MC) system's resistance to carefully crafted inputs in complex real-world communication channels. It simulates real-world conditions and applies two types of subtle modifications: significant amplitude and phase shifts within the same symbol, and shifts between symbols with different modulation methods. A baseline deep learning model is presented, and its behavior under these perturbations is then compared to the performance of GC-GAN and BGAN denoising networks, and a BGAN-Planner that incorporates both. Experimental results show that GCN is highly susceptible to perturbations, while GC-GAN offers limited protection, and BGAN-Planner demonstrates superior resilience in all scenarios tested, notably outperforming competing approaches by a significant margin of over 10% in some cases.

Our research involves developing more efficient tools for the diagnosis of Multiple Sclerosis by utilizing Convolutional Neural Networks and 3D brain images. A key challenge in this field is addressing the varying image styles from different hospitals and protocols. To overcome this issue, we propose training a Convolutional Autoencoder with shared weight parameters. Our experiments demonstrate the training approach and compare the model's performance with traditional methods, including retraining and fine-tuning the model weights from scratch or after pre-training on a large dataset. Our findings reveal that using a continuous learning strategy outperforms these alternatives, achieving a dice score of approximately 0.73 on the MS-LSP14 challenge dataset.

This study introduces an innovative, non-rigorous approach to tackle fractional and linear problems in Sobolev spaces by leveraging unsound mathematical arguments as valid proof techniques. Key problems addressed include proving existence, uniqueness, and obtaining a priori estimates. We leverage known solutions of corresponding dual problems to drive our arguments. Surprisingly, this approach effectively solves one of the most challenging aspects of non-local problems - achieving existence and uniqueness without rigor. Our method is exemplified through a range of questions, including demonstrating the maximum principle, exploring non-local problems with constraints, proving strict suprema and infima attainment, and comparing solutions to fractional problems under specific boundary conditions.

In complex dynamical systems with multiple interacting elements, individual components can be identified, however, understanding how they influence one another remains a significant challenge. Typically, dynamic systems are modeled using mathematical equations, but these models often contain errors. While some basic strategies exist to evaluate the accuracy of a specific component, there's a lack of a more comprehensive approach to identify and understand where models go wrong and how to improve their intelligence in recognizing mistake locations and types. To tackle this issue, we propose a unified framework that integrates the structural and functional aspects of dynamic systems, providing insights into mistake identification and correction. This framework is exemplified through stochastic chemical kinetics, highlighting its practical applicability.

A massive cloud of gas and dust, known as Dragon IRCircumstellar material, is located about 1.3 kiloparsecs away from Earth. It is one of the largest and densest dark nebulae, weighing approximately 10 million times the mass of the sun. It is also home to dense cores that are the birthplaces of new stars. Researchers used data from the Submillimeter Array to study one of these cores called Class I/II source A. They found that this core has a complex structure and develops a core-circumshell structure as it evolves. This evolution could be caused by a developing star pushing dust away from its surroundings or material falling onto the star's surface. If the latter were true, it suggests that this developing star will likely become a massive star when it is born.

Recent advancements in dark energy theories, including models based on black holes formed in the early universe, are being investigated further through the use of the PopSyCLE simulation code. To effectively analyze dark energy theories involving black holes, PopSyCLE has been updated to include a function for integrating the growth of black holes over time. This function is used to model supermassive black hole formation, which is thought to be directly related to dark energy. To ensure accurate integration, the update method and initial conditions are tested, and the updated code is used to determine the relationship between primordial black hole mass and primordial black hole density. This relationship is then used to estimate the redshift at which dark density begins and to compare the results with early universe constraints, providing a way to limit the density of primordial black holes at that point in time.

The behavior of liquid crystals is influenced by their molecular shape, which this study examines using rigid wedge-shaped particles made of spheres. As these particles approach a real liquid crystal's order parameter, our simulations reveal similar structures to those found in liquid crystals, including planar and body-centered tetragonal phases. When the aspect ratio of the wedges is varied, several order-disorder transitions occur, similar to those seen in liquid crystals. One such variation, close to the suggested value for order parameters, led to the appearance of a bcc structure with splay defects, indicating a proximity to the smectic-C* to smectic-E transition, as evidenced by the splay modulation and the structure factor's characteristics.

Our goal is to adjust a model to a new task while keeping a copy of the base model intact for future use. We propose a method called Unique Token Adaptation (UTA), which updates a small set of parameters in the base model to facilitate task-specific updates. In each layer of the base model, we allow only one parameter to take on unique values determined by a task, whereas other parameters remain shared across tasks. We find that UTA outperforms state-of-the-art techniques with minimal additional training parameters. We demonstrate UTA's potential in pre-training a model that can adapt to multiple tasks using a UTA module.

When dealing with the assignment of resources to multiple individuals where each possible combination of sets is viable, a scalar model of preference is challenged due to its inability to account for nuanced preferences. Instead, a partial order model of preference is used, incorporating relations like 'at least as good as'. However, introducing a 'set addition' constraint creates a consistency problem, as demonstrated by researchers in [1]. This study explores how the set addition constraint impacts both non-contextual and contextual preference orderings. We propose a solution to resolve inconsistencies in non-contextual set assignment scenarios, introducing a new concept derived from the dual system approach originally proposed by [2]. This concept is exemplified by examining agent preferences regarding flat apartments with varying layouts.

Recent scientific research has demonstrated a significant correlation between the discovery of thermodynamic properties and kinetic properties of glass-forming mixtures of hydrocarbons and polymers. In this study, the theoretical framework of random free energy landscapes is utilized to develop a predictive model linking temperature and kinetic and thermodynamic parameters. Furthermore, the proposed model allows for the creation of dynamic kinetic curves that can be used to compare systems exhibiting varying glass-forming tendencies. Specifically, the model facilitates the calculation of the ideal glass line in the polymer's phase diagram by creating an equation based on dynamic kinetics. Additionally, the model provides a foundation for developing a generalized kinetic equation suitable for various systems, including hydrocarbons and polymers. Lastly, the calculation techniques described in this study can be applied to real glass-forming systems to establish relationships between thermodynamic-kinetic parameters and the glass-forming mixture composition.

Current language models have a tendency to be overly confident when answering questions. We developed a technique known as Developmental Denial Processing or DDP, which allows transformer models to refuse to provide answers to questions beyond their knowledge and skill set. Implementing this across multiple questions yields consistent results, demonstrating that our approach does not simply rely on detecting uncertainty or a lack of key information. Instead, we found that a single, versatile negative response covers a variety of question categories. Moreover, we found that incorporating developmentally appropriate answers - responses that acknowledge limitations while offering potential solutions or alternative perspectives - significantly enhances model performance across different benchmarks, a development that also has profound implications for human-ai interaction.

In our study, we investigate the effectiveness of attention mechanisms in Neural Machine Translation with production applications. We evaluate three attention mechanisms, including content-based, key-based, and query-based approaches. While attention mechanisms enhance NMT performance by allowing encoder information to be accessed through relevant keys, they may not be as suitable for NMT production due to increased computational complexity and lower quality of key-generated attention distributions. To address this limitation, we propose the Look-forward Attention mechanism, which replaces keys with future states of the decoder to predict the next key. We hypothesize that key quality is a significant factor influencing the performance of attention mechanisms and that look-forward attention can improve production efficiency. Our proposed model achieves better results than existing models with the same or fewer computational resources and a smaller memory footprint. We conduct a comprehensive ablation study to analyze the effectiveness of our approach and provide valuable insights into the behavior of attention mechanisms.

This study calculates the probability measures of Kontsevich graphs linked to the formation of links and introduces the concepts of the link graph, link graph curvature, and the link graph weight for the symplectic Poisson structure. It then derives a general formula for the probability measures of Kontsevich graphs based on these graph curvature concepts.

A specific class of relativistic quantum field theory interactions, which don't preserve thermal conformal symmetry, are present in a large-N expansion of quantum field theories. These interactions become apparent when examining the entanglement entropy scaling in excited states, rather than the ground state. We discover a universal method for calculating an effective thermal conformal anomaly coefficient, which distinguishes interacting theories with their non-relativistic behavior. This coefficient can be calculated using a simple formula in the large-N limit. It turns out that by measuring the entanglement entropy in excited states with a specific UV scale cutoff, rather than analyzing the vacuum state properties, we can determine the strength of these interacting quantum field theories.

The method developed in the 2019 paper "A Comprehensive Framework for Valuing Asian Options under Markov Processes" allows for the valuation of Asian options using grid-based techniques for continuous and discrete types. The approach introduces a new framework for solving nonlinear complementarity problems and stochastic differential complementarity problems, allowing it to handle underlying processes with barriers and jumps. The technique is versatile, able to solve a range of numerical problems, including PDEs and stochastic differential equations, using a unified framework. However, the algorithm contains an error, specifically in the SDCP section under the Continuous Knock-in/Out Cases sub-section. The correct solution should invoke the complementary function G, rather than the barrier level.

This study aims to enhance the constraints on gamma-ray emission from galaxy clusters by analyzing Coma, Perseus and the Hydra-A clusters, which have been observed by the CTA prototype telescope. By collecting a substantial 12.22 stat. and 4.62 syst. counts, we can more accurately quantify the background gamma-ray flux and establish a lower limit of 0.1 TeV. Our findings confirm that the hadronic model is inconsistent with the data at a high statistical significance, while being more in line with lepton interpretations. We estimate a spatial resolution of 0.1° for CTA's observation of these galaxy clusters up to the 0.1 TeV energy level.

The idea of the cosmological collider has been introduced to explore primordial non-Gaussianity in traditional cosmology. Non-Gaussian signals are produced when massive particles interact within a sub-horizonian environment early in the universe, allowing a larger, light particle to scatter off a smaller, heavier particle. This underlying mechanism can be detected through a distinctive pattern of imprints on the primordial curvature perturbation. In this context, certain oscillatory signatures appear only along specific directions, such as those linked to the mass of the interacting particle or its spin. Moreover, traditional non-Gaussian signals exhibit a characteristic, circular symmetry, while the underlying physics of particle collisions can be further understood through a connection with random matrix theory.

Despite achieving state-of-the-art performance, Deep Convolutional Neural Networks still operate as a black box, making interpretability a significant issue. Recent efforts to uncover the inner workings of these models have yielded some success, but a more comprehensive understanding of their functional aspects is still needed. In this research, a new approach is proposed to analyze how DCNNs process and transform visual inputs through their intermediate layers. By using a method that integrates visual semantics, our approach successfully reveals a hierarchical structure of detection and discrimination filters, where the initial layers focus on identifying basic features and subsequent layers progressively integrate this information to differentiate nuanced characteristics. This study provides new insights into how DCNNs process complex images and sheds light on their internal representation capabilities.

We utilize the path integral Monte Carlo simulation to investigate one-dimensional high-Tc superconducting cuprates, where we perform full-dimensional simulations of electrons and phonons to examine how electrons interact with phonons in these materials. Notably, our results indicate that an attractive force emerges when an electron traverses the anti-nodes of phonons with frequencies within a specific range - typically lower than those phonons that normally scatter electrons in one-dimensional systems. Furthermore, the balance between phonons that repel and attract electrons is influenced by factors such as electron density and temperature, which favor attraction under conditions of lower temperatures and higher electron density. Ultimately, our findings support the hypothesis that phonon-assigned long-distance attractive interactions among electrons can serve as a potential driving mechanism for high-Tc superconductivity in the cuprates.

This study examines a detailed dataset from the Multi-Purpose Household and Industry Survey, which encompasses information on establishments and wage employees in Manabí Province, Ecuador. We investigate potential labor supply suppression caused by existing employment, which is often referred to as the "discouraged worker effect." Utilizing available data, we develop a multilevel model to mitigate sampling bias and employ the X-LASSO method to uncover underlying causal relationships between establishment-level and employee-level characteristics. Our analysis reveals that establishments with lower educational requirements and those with higher working conditions have a significant impact on establishing relationships among absent and present worker data.

We discovered a unique metastability in the crystal structure of the chiral magnet Co$_9$Zn$_9$Mn$_2$ that persists for an extended period. Specifically, the lattice's metastable phase, typically associated with magnetic patterns, can be physically seen under microscopic examination. Notably, the Co$_9$Zn$_9$Mn$_2$ sample can maintain both its metastable lattice structure and magnetic properties for at least three months at low temperatures, allowing both to be naturally preserved without being influenced by an applied magnetic field. By utilizing neutron diffraction techniques, our findings demonstrate that the metastable lattice structure exhibits significantly higher stability compared to its equilibrium state. Moreover, the metastable lattice structure can be triggered by heating the sample to 150 K and subsequently cooled, showcasing a first-order structural transition. Furthermore, the metastable lattice structure exhibits a distinct temperature dependence in magnetic properties that differs from its equilibrium counterpart, indicating that the metastable state is not merely a result of thermal fluctuations. Notably, the metastable state's magnetic properties are also found to be distinct from those of the equilibrium state, indicating that the metastable state is a distinct thermodynamic phase.

Social networks and influence propagation are key areas of study in the social sciences, yet a major limitation persists in the existing literature when dealing with social networks that have a large number of nodes and are dynamic in nature. In order to address this gap, a selective review is provided of the methods employed in the literature to model influence propagation in high-dimensional dynamic social networks, with a focus on the main approaches and their associated strategies, including: a) regression-based models that account for time-varying coefficients through the use of penalization, smoothing techniques, and other related methods; b) model-based frameworks that integrate latent factor models, model-based clustering, and other clustering methods; and c) network propagation models, which model the evolution of node states over time. In addition to providing an overview of these approaches, the review also highlights the main challenges and future avenues of research associated with them, with a focus on the use of different forms of network data, the use of network models that capture non-stationary and non-independent behaviors, and the development of models that can explain the mechanisms underlying influence propagation in unobserved networks.

This paper explores an algorithm based on stable configurations to address the balance problem. A key feature of this method is that it guarantees a locally optimal solution with a girth of at least three, which is guaranteed to be within a polynomial factor of the global optimum. Specifically, the achieved approximation factor is at most $\Theta(\log n)$, where $n$ signifies the total weight of all leaves.

A recently developed technique called Bayesian Neural Networks (BNN) has shown potential in creating reliable cover-steganography by leveraging cover content in a learnable and statistical manner. This non-reversible, reversible-like approach uses binned confidence levels to represent secret data in BNN predictions, allowing for reversible hiding when novel content is available. However, existing BNN-captured data is not suitable for direct communication. This research proposes the use of reversible hiding within BNN-predictions, but the raw data must first be transformed using lossless compression, dispersion, and diffusion. The method's effectiveness, along with its and the original approach's superior performance compared to traditional steganography methods, is validated and demonstrated. The associated source code and examples can be accessed at https://github.com/alexgurevich/BNNSteg.

A key aspect of numerical dynamo models is their kineitic turbulence spectrum, which is often lost when transitioning to reduced models like mean-field approaches. These reduced models typically lose the turbulent back-reaction on the large-scale dynamo. We demonstrate through simulations that this limitation is significant. To address this issue, we suggest utilizing the spectrum provided by dynamical alpha and Omega effects as a sign that the turbulent influences are being accurately represented.

A vast nearby starburst galaxy, NGC4945, is characterized by an intense and widespread star formation activity. Observations using ALMA reveal the presence of a powerful outflow originating from the central region of the galaxy, moving at speeds of approximately 500 to 700 km/s at a distance of 200 pc. The outflow's mass is estimated to be around 10 to 30 solar masses, based on ALMA's data of CO and SO molecules. A theoretical model suggests a connection between the outflow and intense star formation within the galaxy's center, with a star formation rate of around 1-3 solar masses per year potentially driving the outflow. The outflow's total energy is around 10 to 30 x 10^51 ergs, indicating a need for additional sources, such as black hole activity or collective star activity, to sustain it. The outflow's properties are compared with existing data from a nearby starburst galaxy, M82, to provide further insights.

A sophisticated numerical algorithm known as Galerkin produces inherently stable solutions by satisfying discrete energy laws by design. However, implementing this method for magnetized plasma problems often presents challenges due to the complex nature of quasilinear diffusion operators, particularly when employing finite element spaces. To overcome these difficulties, a new approach has been developed by introducing a stream function formulation for finite element models and incorporating specialized formulations for key quantities, particularly in one and two-dimensional settings. A comprehensive analysis has been carried out on the resulting algorithm's discrete energy properties and numerical tests have confirmed its effectiveness and accuracy. Moreover, the non-symmetric characteristics of this formulation are shown to yield a discrete equivalent of the continuous energy conservation law, thereby ensuring strict stability and preserving positivity even in the absence of artificial dissipation. This novel approach is particularly advantageous for problems involving intricate magnetic magnetic gradients.

For standard ordinary differential equations, it's established that differential equations with derivative powers greater than one can still have stable equilibrium solutions, though they may not necessarily have all real eigenvalues. This study focuses on developing and evaluating a variable stepsize Second Derivative Integrator Multiplier method for improving the efficiency of IM method-based algorithms in this context. Key outcomes include providing necessary conditions for stability, presenting a high-order method formulation, and demonstrating through numerical experiments that these variable stepsize methods offer enhanced stability compared to constant stepsize IM methods.

In a Banach space semigroup setting, we establish a criterion based on Lyapunov conditions for exponential stability, while ensuring this stability remains robust in a broader sense. Our method involves a novel approach utilizing a specific, previously underused condition in Lyapunov theory.

To aid the muon-based enhancement experiments, we have developed MuMuPy, a software package, to simulate the interaction of dimuonium atoms with matter. This tool computes key parameters: the dimuonium radius, diffusion length, and reaction rate. Using the Schr\"odinger equation, we model the ground state of the muon-muonium ($\mu^+ \mu^-$ H) system and determine its properties by estimating the energy levels. This computation takes into account the finite masses of the muon and muonium in dimuonium molecules. The diffusion length and reaction rate are determined through a combination of previously published studies and specific experiments. The results show that dimuonium-based concepts yield promising muon-based enhancement possibilities due to the significantly larger dimuonium radius compared to positronium-based systems, thus increasing the probability of the desired reaction.

This paper seamlessly integrates two existing frameworks: one by Merton for an investor-agnostic model and the other by Cuoco and Van Campenhout for a relative wealth model with logarithmic utility. The combined model considers both absolute and relative wealth utilities, with the latter having a power form. The study finds a critical threshold for the aversion coefficient where investment strategies change abruptly. The analysis provides optimal portfolio strategies under the assumption that market parameters are known.

The cosmic evolution of dwarf galaxies is intricately linked to the evolution of their surrounding intergalactic and interstellar mediums. However, the halo virial radius of dwarf galaxies often presents observational challenges due to their relatively small sizes and fainter brightness. As such, astronomers must develop novel techniques to obtain cleaner observations of these neighboring regions. We aim to enhance the understanding of how dwarf galaxies interact with and evolve through the intergalactic medium by drawing on existing data and theoretical predictions regarding early galaxy formation. We will also investigate how to identify stripped or pre-stripped intergalactic halos around dwarf galaxies and discuss future prospects for observing these regions with the James Webb Space Telescope.

We examine the interplay between a non-local, sub-linear bosonic field and fermions under conditions of sub-Kepleric dynamics, where the exponents $\alpha$ and $\mu$ for the bosonic and bosonic field couplings satisfy $\alpha < 2\mu+1$. Our perturbation analysis of the corresponding many-body Schrödinger equation reveals an unconventional behavior in the resulting low-energy spectrum. Firstly, unlike typical low-energy dynamics observed in similar systems, the dispersion relation for the emergent low-energy states is not a power law but forms a parabolic curve $\epsilon \sim k^2$. This similarity to the non-relativistic Schrödinger equation is attributed to a non-local interaction. Secondly, the spectrum's structure suggests a non-zero binding energy between fermions and antiparticles at the Fermi surface due to this interaction, giving rise to a concept akin to molecular orbitals derived from bound states of fermions and antiparticles. We predict this effect using the Dirac equation, which exhibits the same non-locality and dynamic characteristics and molecular analogy.
We determine the exact asymptotic growth rates for the groups $G_n^\pm$ within the broader Thompson group hierarchy, as well as for the twisted and braided versions of the Thompson groups.

This article introduces the refinement of the REtrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) framework, utilizing the DistilBERT cross-encoder DPR retriever, through the AdvertiseAds dataset for question-answer pairs. Initially, we assess the efficacy of the DPR retriever by comparing its performance against the default DPR retriever's results. Following this evaluation, we proceed with the refinement process, adopting the AdvertiseAds dataset as our reference point.

This study calculates the long-term behavior of the recurrence coefficients, polynomials, and Niemi functions associated with polynomials that are orthogonal relative to a specific function involving two parameters. A disruption in the original measure's orthogonality conditions occurs when one of the parameters reaches a specific threshold. The approach used to determine this behavior is the two-parameter family's connection to Ulam's stochastic process. Ulam's process is characterized by a singular behavior where its equilibrium density has a specific functional form with parameters taking infinite and zero values. A specific case of the original measure where the parameters take on opposite extreme values can be approximated using the general two-parameter case, and this allows for determining the orthogonal polynomials' behavior in the limit.

In this research, we present a novel assessment designed to evaluate the capacity of human annotators in identifying key themes within longer passages, aiming to enhance the quality of annotation and data collection for automated text summarization. Our annotation process focuses on human feedback, which is crucial in determining the quality of machine-generated summaries and can also offer insights into human narrative understanding when compared to machine summarization performance. We discovered that identifying skilled annotators for this task among a large pool of Turkers is akin to searching for a needle in a large haystack, and as a result, we developed a series of verification methods to ensure the reliability of our collected annotations.

Text-video retrieval systems rely on accurate feature representation, which can be compromised by irrelevancy in visual content and misalignment between text and visual cues. To address this issue, our proposed approach leverages the flexibility of the Transformer architecture to develop an adaptive feature representation module that selectively filters irrelevant features from videos and enables dynamic interaction between sequential video features and corresponding text features. Furthermore, our enhancement of the Transformer with a token shift mechanism allows for a deeper, dynamic capture of complex text-video relationships. Experimental findings demonstrate that TS2-Net outperforms existing state-of-the-art techniques by a substantial margin, significantly surpassing competitors by over 4 in mRec@10 and over 5 in mRec@20 protocols.

We have investigated neutral currents that change quark flavors and link top quarks to light quarks, which are not permitted by the Standard Model but could be found in theories beyond it. The production and decay of these quarks in pairs (ttbar) would be significantly different in the presence of these neutral currents. Specifically, we've derived an expression for how often tXbarY production occurs in collisions of high-energy quarks (where X and Y are either charm or strange quarks) and how frequently tXbar Ybar decay happens. Additionally, we've estimated how often the final result involves four quarks (quark quark quark quark) is produced when there are neutral currents involved. Using actual data from the LHC, we've created theoretical predictions for the ratio of certain production and decay events and then considered how accurate detectors can be in measuring these ratios.

Building on previous research, we've analyzed the structure of an initially-tiny random network, where each new addition connects to existing nodes based on a modified probability formula. This modification involves a random yet preferential component, allowing us to study various network models by adjusting the influence of preferential attachment relative to random attachments. We've derived a general distribution for the sizes of node degrees in networks with directed edges, revealing how these degrees behave asymptotically in different models and identifying conditions under which a network's structure is dominated by preferential attachment. Our findings also show that certain models exhibit more heterogeneous degree distributions than others. However, we've found that when preferential attachment has a strong influence, networks with preferential attachments tend to have smaller average path lengths and a higher clustering coefficient than those with random connections.

A network-based approach using a convolutional neural network (CNN) can recognize disturbances affecting a mannequin's pose by analyzing pressure distribution on its surface via 9x9 electrode grids, wireless disturbance sensing (WDS) technology. The research involves training an eight-class CNN model that not only classifies various disturbances affecting the sensor but also identifies different types of human interferences, incorporating pose estimation data from the sensor and a self-tracking mannequin. Initially, an eight-layer CNN was developed and trained on 10-fold cross-validation, achieving an average accuracy of 96%. Subsequently, a three-layer CNN was designed and evaluated on a benchmark dataset from the 2020 DRUIDS challenge, achieving an average accuracy of 97.5% for testing datasets. Furthermore, the model's parameters were optimized using the three-opt genetic algorithm, yielding an average accuracy of 97.7% and significantly reducing the model's complexity by over 50%.

To spacetime models incorporating cosmic strings, multiple approaches have been taken into consideration. One specific framework that considers the spacetime as displaced along a direction perpendicular to the string has not yet been extensively studied until now. A displacement parameter in the spacetime metric was first introduced by Pal and Som, leading to the Som-Palaniswami-Raychaudhuri spacetime model. Researchers proposed an alternative version where parameter 'a' represents the gravitational field's effect in the spacetime as well as cosmic strings. 'a' is now assumed to be space-like in the Som-Raychaudhuri spacetime, allowing us to analyze its implications. To investigate this further, research focused on examining how certain physical quantities such as energy, charge, and a specific factor known as the vorticity parameter are interrelated in relation to the displacement parameter 'a'.

This paper examines algebras of real-valued measurable sets equipped with specific metrics, including the Ferrers metric, a natural topology, and the relativized metric. It defines and investigates the property of local normality within these algebras and its relationship with other known characteristics, including normability, complete homogeneity, and normality. Additionally, the study provides essential criteria and, primarily, space-like criteria for various types of measurable algebras to be considered complete with the Ferrers metric, as well as for inducing a topology that makes the algebra a topological group.

We've developed a new helicity observable in transverse-virtual Compton scattering, $I_{1+}$, that can effectively separate it from other processes and from a combination of a boson exchange and the spin-flip structure function. Our analysis shows that this novel observable, $I_{1+}$, can distinguish the spin-flip structure function, $F_{5,5}$, from the other spin-dependent structure functions, $F_{2,5}$ and $F_{1,5}$. Furthermore, by comparing $F_{5,5}$ with the other structure functions, we can gain insights into the baryon form factors, $G_{A, Q, G}$, in a way that is invariant under gauge transformations. Our calculations demonstrate that, given current experimental uncertainties in the measurement of $F_{5,5}$, an accurate determination of $F_{5,5}$ is feasible within a few percent. This can be achieved through experiments involving circularly polarized light and a hydrogen target, as demonstrated by proposed setups at JLab and the EIC.

Artificial Intelligence has numerous applications, and its efficiency can be
augmented, depending on the field, by incorporating data and knowledge,
thereby giving rise to Enhanced Artificial Intelligence. To facilitate this
process, a structured framework is proposed to integrate knowledge and
artificial intelligence within various domains.

We investigate the thermal properties of spin-orbit coupled correlated bosons using a quasiclassical approach, where we derive a self-consistent equation for the single-particle energy spectrum, taking into account finite-temperature effects on superfluid-dinsuperfluid transition in optical lattices. We study the influence of temperature on the transition by examining the behavior of the superfluid transition temperature as a function of its critical points. Our findings, validated by comparisons with full numerical calculations, reveal that the superfluid transition temperature is significantly affected by orbital fluctuations. We also investigate the impact of orbital fluctuations on the superfluid ground state and its response to thermal excursions, and discuss how these findings can be experimentally probed using lattice-based thermal shifts in thermal shifts of the superfluid transition.

Graph theory in relation to groups has been an active field of study, and a specific sub-area focuses on graph models based on finite abelian groups, known as FAGGs. A notable sub-area within FAGGs is the graph model known as the well-known Cayley graph. A notable question in this field is the set of possible chromatic values for a finite abelian group of order $n$, denoted as $\mathcal{C}_n$. A recent paper, graphically characterized all possible distance-$2$ graphs formed using finite abelian groups with order under $50$.

This study explores various aspects of the AdS/CFT correspondence in low-dimensional settings by examining the interactions of N units of Type IIA string with k-branes, where N and k are coprime,
 
 Our research reveals that this configuration leads to an AdS$_4$ space with SU(2) isometry and SU(3) boundary current algebra content on the dual string theory.
 
 In addition, we investigate the effects of adding additional k-branes and find that the geometry and dual theory remain unchanged, whereas incorporating NS5-branes results in an S$^3$/A_2 quotient space that is fibered over AdS$_4$ and gives rise to a level-N SU(2)$_R$ current algebra content.

Researchers have been developing novel kernel functions by analyzing mathematical equations in relation to Gaussian Processes, and these kinetic kernel functions exhibit exceptional properties. When applied to binary classification tasks, they demonstrate performance on par with leading classifications methods such as logistic regression, support vector machines, and neural networks. Moreover, they significantly outperform existing Gaussian Process kernels, particularly on datasets with numerous features or high intrinsic noise levels.

Achieving beam-induced noise mitigation at muon colliders is a crucial challenge for a successful experiment. A comparative analysis of various beam noise reduction techniques was conducted, focusing on two major issues: the long-term consequences of beam dispersion and the immediate impact of beam dispersion on the detector's sensitivity. By leveraging theoretical models and using realistic muon collider beam conditions, this study evaluated the performance of different noise reduction methods and assessed their impact on beam dispersion, ultimately generating one-dimensional signal-to-background ratios to determine the effectiveness of each technique. The results indicate that a combination of two noise reduction methods, namely muon cooling and using thick target stacks, is the most effective strategy for minimizing beam-induced detector damage.

We propose a novel regularization technique that can be integrated into deep learning frameworks to reduce memory usage and compute requirements by allowing the calculation and storage of neural networks to be flexible. This method can be used in conjunction with existing pruning techniques and is effective even with pre-trained models, demonstrating its value as a standalone solution. The potential of this method lies in its ability to be combined with other model compression approaches and is a promising direction for future research.

In certain systems with bosonic structure, a phenomenon known as Pauli obstruction arises and results in a significant reduction of sound speed to zero. This behavior is typically seen in strongly interacting Bose-Einstein condensates near the Bose obstruction limit. However, it has been found that it can also occur in weakly interacting Bose fluids. Our study examines the emergence of Pauli obstruction in these weakly interacting fluids. Using the Bogoliubov approximation to describe interactions and numerical solutions to the resulting equations, we found that in systems with tetrahedral lattice structures, the emergence of Pauli obstruction is associated with a critical point where the longitudinal sound mode becomes unstable and reaches an inflection point. This phenomenon is characterized by the appearance of a flat mode localized at the Brillouin zone boundary, which corresponds to the emergence of a van Hove singularity at the Fermi surface. Our results indicate that the emergence of Pauli obstruction in weakly interacting fluids is associated with the approach of a van Hove singularity to the Fermi surface.

This article presents a survey-based investigation into how software developers assess 
the quality criteria known as test odors within unit tests. Survey responses provided 
insights into whether and to what extent developers consider test odor issues critical.
The survey targeted whether developers generally regard test odor problems as critical, 
whether they see them as critical in the context of their own organizations, and whether 
developers experience test odor problems. A total of 50 responses were received from 
a non-randomized group of software developers who use Java unit testing. The results 
reveal that nearly half of developers perceive test odor issues as critical in general 
and in their organizations specifically. Moreover, nearly half developers reported 
experiencing test odor issues with varying degrees of impact. The findings suggest that 
unit test quality may require greater attention from the software development team.

This paper introduces a general sweeping procedure to handle nonconvex sets that comprise clusters of areas connected by thin corridors, forming either in multiple dimensions or in the form of a line. Firstly, we study its properties relative to the complement of this set and develop a novel integral-differential criterion to identify the projection of a point onto the connected components of the boundary. This criterion is subsequently applied in two different contexts, one involving multiple clusters in a multidimensional space, driven by a search-theory based case study to identify local maxima within specific constraints on the dimensions, and another scenario set in a one-dimensional domain, where it is used in conjunction with an optimization technique on curves to identify sharp features while minimizing the deviation from the original curve.

The Monte Carlo event creator KKMCee has been updated to include simulations of lepton and quark pair production at lepton colliders up to  TeV energy levels, which  includes simulations of $e^+e^-$, $e^{\mu}^{\mu} $, $e^{2}\to \nu\bar{\nu}^{+}$, $e^{2}\to \ell\ell^{+}$, and $e^{2}\to q\bar{q}^{+}$ processes at leading order QED.  These simulations incorporate multi-photon emissions up to next-to-leading order (NLO) and an additional set of simulations for multi-photon emissions for the $e^+e^-$ process.  Multi-photon emissions are included for lepton and quark pair production at lepton colliders up to lepton colliders up to  TeV energy levels, which is necessary for precise simulations of these processes.
